title: The Abhidhamma's seven books
hook: a walk along the seven books of the Abhidhamma, ending in the great book of conditions
carry: seven books, ending in the web of conditions

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Abhidhamma, the higher teaching: the mind laid out like a watch on a cloth. Your line: the smallest parts.

Before anyone reads a book, there's the spine on the shelf. A title, nothing more, and already it tells you something. The third basket is made of seven books, and their titles read like a strange little poem. A list. An analysis. A talk about elements. A book of persons. A book of arguments. A book of pairs. And the great book of conditions. Today, no deep dive: just a slow walk along the shelf, pulling each book out far enough to see how it begins.
screen: `SEVEN SPINES ON A SHELF.` → `A STRANGE LITTLE POEM.` → `A WALK ALONG THE SHELF.`

segments.voice: First, the Dhammasangani, the enumeration of things. It opens with the list of mental states, wholesome, unwholesome and neither, then takes a single wholesome moment and names everything present in it. Second, the Vibhanga, the book of analysis. It takes familiar teachings, the aggregates, the senses, the noble truths, and analyzes each one, often first in the style of the suttas and then in the Abhidhamma's own. Third, the Dhatukatha, the discussion of elements: how each thing fits, or doesn't, into the larger groupings. Fourth, a surprise: the Puggalapannatti, the designation of persons. In a basket that takes people apart into moments, here's a whole book sorting kinds of people: the one who keeps a promise, the one who doesn't. In two days, this path will show why that's no contradiction. Fifth, the Kathavatthu, the points of controversy, where the views of other early Buddhist schools are set out and answered, one argument at a time. Tradition says it was put together at a council long after the Buddha, by an elder named Moggaliputta Tissa, following an outline the Buddha had laid down. Sixth, the Yamaka, the book of pairs. It asks its questions forward and backward: is every this a that, and is every that a this? A book about using words exactly. And seventh, the Patthana, the book of conditions, which tradition calls the great book. It asks how each thing helps another arise: by being its root, by coming just before it, by supporting it. Tradition says that when the Buddha turned his mind to it, colored light streamed from his body.
screen: `THE LIST OF MENTAL STATES.` · `A BOOK THAT SORTS PERSONS.` · `A BOOK OF ARGUMENTS AND PAIRS.` · then, large: `THE GREAT BOOK OF CONDITIONS.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, say the seven titles inwardly, one for each slow breath, in English or in Pali: the enumeration of things, analysis, elements, persons, points of controversy, pairs, conditions. Then rest on the last one, and notice one thing in this moment that something else helped bring about: the warmth of the chair, the light from the window, this breath.
Seven books. The third basket of the Pali canon, from the list of mental states to the great book of conditions. Today's word.
Your line: seven books, ending in the web of conditions. A list of mental states at the start; at the end, each moment leaning on others. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada monks and nuns study the seven books of the Abhidhamma, and in some Theravada communities passages from them, including the opening list of the Dhammasangani, are chanted at ceremonies.

chat.meaning: The Abhidhamma basket holds seven books, from the Dhammasangani's list of mental states to the Patthana, the great book of conditions. In some Theravada communities their openings are chanted at ceremonies, funerals among them.

tie.story: Tradition says that when the Buddha turned his mind to the Patthana, the great book of conditions, colored light streamed from his body.

notes: The count 'seven books' is the index's title; the seven are named in the Abhidhamma Pitaka itself.

The Kathavatthu: tradition (Atthasalini; also the Mahavamsa and Dipavamsa accounts of the third council) ties it to Moggaliputta Tissa at a council under Ashoka, following an outline (matika) laid down by the Buddha. 'Long after the Buddha' kept vague on purpose; confirm wording.
The rays of colored light when the Buddha contemplated the Patthana come from the Atthasalini (usually told as six-colored rays); the number was cut under the claims rule. Confirm.
Vibhanga 'often first in the style of the suttas and then in the Abhidhamma's own style' (suttantabhajaniya / abhidhammabhajaniya). Confirm wording.
howItsDone: chanting the Dhammasangani matika at ceremonies (e.g. funerals in Thailand and Myanmar) — confirm and soften if needed.
